Using rdantic with ellmer

Source: vignettes/ellmer.Rmd
ellmer.Rmd
library(rdantic)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'rdantic'
#> The following object is masked from 'package:graphics':
#> 
#>     frame
#> The following object is masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     date
library(ellmer)

This vignette assumes that chat is an ellmer chat object that has already been created and configured. The examples use the same structured extraction task in two styles: an ellmer type specification, and an rdantic declaration converted to an ellmer type.

The same type, side by side

Suppose a model should return a person’s name and positive age. With ellmer, the response type is assembled directly from ellmer’s type_*() functions:

ellmer_type <- type_object(
  age = type_integer(),
  name = type_string()
)

answer_ellmer <- chat$chat_structured(
  "My name is Bob and I'm 30 years old",
  type = ellmer_type
)
answer_ellmer
#> $age
#> [1] 30
#>
#> $name
#> [1] "Bob"

The equivalent rdantic declaration keeps the same shape available as an R type. [1] says that each field is a scalar, and [. > 0] adds a validation rule to age:

AgeName <- struct(
  .name = "AgeName",
  .description = "A structure representing a person's age and name",
  age = (int[1][. > 0] | NULL),
  name = (chr[1] | NULL)
)
AgeName
#> <struct> AgeName
#>   age  : int[1][. > 0] | NULL
#>   name : chr[1] | NULL

Convert the declaration at the boundary where ellmer needs its type:

answer_rdantic <- chat$chat_structured(
  "My name is Bob and I'm 30 years old",
  type = to_ellmer_type(AgeName)
)
answer_rdantic
#> $age
#> [1] 30
#>
#> $name
#> [1] "Bob"

If we want to check the answer with rdantic, we can do so with from_list().

checked_answer <- from_list(AgeName, answer_rdantic)
checked_answer
#> <AgeName>
#>   age  : 30L
#>   name : "Bob"

This is better illustrated with a text that doesnt conform to the age > 0 requirement.

answer_invalid <- chat$chat_structured(
  "My name is Alice and I'm -5 years old",
  type = to_ellmer_type(AgeName)
)
answer_invalid
#> $age
#> [1] -5
#>
#> $name
#> [1] "Alice"

from_list(AgeName, answer_invalid)
#> Error: 1 validation problem in AgeName
#>   $age  expected int[1][. > 0] | NULL, got int[1] -5L

to_ellmer_type() is equivalent to the longer form:

to_ellmer_type(AgeName)
# is equivalent to
AgeName |>
  rdantic::schema() |>
  rdantic::to_json() |>
  ellmer::type_from_schema()

And the to_ellmer_type() result is identical to the ellmer type that would be constructed manually using type_from_schema().

AgeName <- struct(
  .name = "AgeName",
  .description = "A structure representing a person's age and name",
  age = (int[1][. > 0] | NULL),
  name = (chr[1] | NULL)
)

ellmer_age_name <- ellmer::type_object(
  age = type_integer(),
  name = type_string()
)

all.equal(to_ellmer_type(AgeName), ellmer_age_name)
#> [1] "target is ellmer::TypeJsonSchema, current is ellmer::TypeObject"

# note the ellmer type is different, so we need to do some further cosmetic adjustments
# to actually compare the values

from_rdantic <- to_ellmer_type(AgeName)
from_ellmer <- ellmer_age_name

# Both interfaces expose the same response fields and scalar types.
ellmer_properties <- S7::prop(from_ellmer, "properties")
rdantic_schema <- S7::prop(from_rdantic, "json")

all.equal(names(ellmer_properties), names(rdantic_schema$properties))
#> [1] TRUE
all.equal(
  vapply(ellmer_properties, function(x) S7::prop(x, "type"), character(1)),
  vapply(rdantic_schema$properties, function(x) {
    if (!is.null(x$type)) x$type[[1]] else x$anyOf[[1]]$type
  }, character(1))
)
#> [1] TRUE

The adapter also accepts a schema that has already been created:

age_name_schema <- schema(AgeName)
answer_rdantic <- chat$chat_structured(
  "My name is Bob and I'm 30 years old",
  type = to_ellmer_type(age_name_schema)
)
answer_rdantic
#> $age
#> [1] 30
#>
#> $name
#> [1] "Bob"

Required fields and nullable values

rdantic distinguishes between a field that is required and a field whose value may be NULL. In the declaration above, both fields accept NULL, so an rdantic constructor may omit them. This is useful when validating ordinary R records, but ellmer’s structured response format requires every property name to appear in the JSON Schema required array.

to_ellmer_type() adapts the schema for that boundary: age and name are both required response properties, while their schemas still allow null. The model should therefore return both keys, using null when a value cannot be provided.

rdantic_schema <- schema(AgeName)
rdantic_schema$required
#> list()

ellmer_schema <- S7::prop(to_ellmer_type(AgeName), "json")
ellmer_schema$required
#> [[1]]
#> [1] "age"
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] "name"
ellmer_schema$properties$age$type
#> NULL

# JSON arrays are represented as lists after ellmer parses the schema.
rdantic_schema$required <- as.list(names(rdantic_schema$properties))
rdantic_schema$properties$name$type <- as.list(rdantic_schema$properties$name$type)
all.equal(ellmer_schema, rdantic_schema)
#> [1] TRUE

The original rdantic schema is not modified. The stricter required handling is applied only to the schema passed to ellmer.

Nested records

The same conversion works for nested structs and arrays of structs. Declare the inner record once, then use it in the outer declaration:

Address <- struct(
  .name = "Address",
  city = chr[1] | NULL,
  country = chr[1] | NULL
)

Person <- struct(
  .name = "Person",
  name = chr[1] | NULL,
  address = Address | NULL,
  previous_addresses = list_of(Address)
)

The nested object schemas are normalized as well, including the object inside previous_addresses:

converted <- S7::prop(to_ellmer_type(Person), "json")
converted$required
#> [[1]]
#> [1] "name"
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] "address"
#> 
#> [[3]]
#> [1] "previous_addresses"
converted$properties$address$anyOf[[1]]$required
#> [[1]]
#> [1] "city"
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] "country"
converted$properties$previous_addresses$items$required
#> [[1]]
#> [1] "city"
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] "country"

Pass the converted type to ellmer exactly as before:

answer <- chat$chat_structured(
  "Bob lives in Paris and previously lived in Berlin",
  type = to_ellmer_type(Person)
)

#__TODO__

Validate the response in R

The ellmer response is typed for the model call, but the rdantic declaration can remain the application’s validation boundary. By default, chat$chat_structured() uses convert = TRUE and returns an R list. Validate that list with from_list():

answer <- list(
  name = "Bob",
  address = list(city = "Paris", country = "France"),
  previous_addresses = list(list(city = "Berlin", country = "Germany"))
)

person <- from_list(Person, answer)
person$name
#> [1] "Bob"
person$address$city
#> [1] "Paris"

When convert = FALSE, ellmer returns the structured response as JSON text. That form can be validated with from_json() instead:

reply <- '{
  "name": "Bob",
  "address": {"city": "Paris", "country": "France"},
  "previous_addresses": [{"city": "Berlin", "country": "Germany"}]
}'

person_from_json <- from_json(Person, reply)
person_from_json$name
#> [1] "Bob"

This gives one declaration for both sides of the integration: to_ellmer_type() produces the response type that ellmer needs, while from_list() or from_json() applies rdantic’s coercion and validation rules after the response arrives.
